questions.statement: "Is the library open on Sunday?" she asked. She asked if the library ___ on Sunday.
questions.context: A polar question reported with if.

options.feedback: Correct! A polar question becomes a statement word order, so the subject comes before the auxiliary.
The question word order cannot survive inside a reported clause, because that clause is a statement.
Were is the form of the second conditional and is not used for a library opening on a real Sunday.
A present perfect would suggest the question was about a period up to now, and Sunday is a stated day.

questions.explanation:
A reported polar question takes the word order of a statement: subject, auxiliary, rest. The auxiliary keeps the tense the reporter uses.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Have you finished the report?" he asked. He asked whether I ___ the report.
questions.context: A polar question with a present perfect, backshifted.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect backshifts to the past perfect when the reporting verb is in the past.
Keeping the present perfect would mean the reporting verb was also present.
A past continuous would describe an action under way, which the original question does not.
A bare base form would leave the clause without a tense of its own.

questions.explanation:
Backshift also applies to the perfect tenses. The present perfect moves to the past perfect, and the question word order becomes statement word order.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Where do they sell the tickets?" she asked. She asked where they ___ the tickets.
questions.context: A wh question about a place, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! The wh question keeps its question word and the clause takes the word order of a statement.
The auxiliary do cannot remain in a reported statement clause; the tense is already carried by the reporting verb.
A present continuous would describe an action under way, and the original question is about the usual arrangement.
The past simple would backshift a present simple twice, and the question is reported in the present.

questions.explanation:
In a reported wh question the auxiliary disappears and the main verb takes the form the reporter's tense requires. The question word stays at the front.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Who called you?" she asked. She asked who ___ her.
questions.context: A question about a person, with the verb backshifted.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple call backshifts to the past perfect with a past reporting verb.
Calls is the present form and shows no backshift at all.
A base form would need an auxiliary to carry the tense, and none is present in the clause.
A future form would place the call after the moment of asking, which the past reporting verb excludes.

questions.explanation:
Backshift moves the tense one step back even in a wh question. The only change to the structure is the loss of the question word order.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Didn't you get my message?" he asked. He asked whether I ___ his message.
questions.context: A negative polar question reported with whether.

options.feedback: Correct! The negative auxiliary did becomes had not when the tense is backshifted.
Keeping didn't would ignore the backshift that every other tense undergoes in this report.
A present perfect would place the receiving in the present period, and the reporting verb is past.
A would would turn the question into a hypothetical, and the original was a plain query.

questions.explanation:
In a negative question, the auxiliary did is the tense carrier, so backshift changes it to had and moves the not with it. The main verb then takes the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Are they going to cancel the trip?" she asked. She asked whether they ___ to cancel the trip.
questions.context: A question about something not yet decided, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! Be going to backshifts its first auxiliary, so are becomes were, while going keeps its form.
Keeping are going would require a present reporting verb, and she asked is in the past.
A past perfect would shift the whole structure, and the original are going to needs only one step.
A will is a different future form and would change the meaning of the plan.

questions.explanation:
Only the first auxiliary of a compound future shifts. In are going to cancel, the are becomes were and the rest of the phrase is untouched.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "When does the train leave?" he asked. He asked when the train ___.
questions.context: A wh question about a time, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! A future simple backshifts to would plus base verb in reported speech.
The auxiliary does is removed in a reported clause, and it cannot be kept to carry the tense.
The past simple would backshift a past simple, and the original is a present form.
A present perfect would place the departure inside the present period, and the question is about a schedule.

questions.explanation:
A question about a timetable reports naturally with would, because the reporter is looking at the same question from an earlier moment in time.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Why are you laughing?" she asked. She asked why I ___.
questions.context: A question about a reason, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! The present continuous backshifts to the past continuous in a reported question.
Keeping the present would require a present reporting verb, and she asked is in the past.
The past simple would backshift a past simple, and the original is a continuous form.
A past perfect would shift twice and change the meaning from ongoing to completed.

questions.explanation:
The continuous tenses also backshift. Present continuous becomes past continuous, which is why she asked why I was laughing reads naturally.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Can you drive a lorry?" he asked. He asked whether I ___ drive a lorry.
questions.context: A question with a modal, which does not change form.

options.feedback: Correct! Can backshifts to could because it is a modal that has a direct past equivalent.
Keeping can would require a present reporting verb, and the question is reported in the past.
May expresses permission rather than ability, and the original question is about ability.
A would would build a conditional, and the original is a plain question about capability.

questions.explanation:
A few modals do have a past equivalent, and those do shift: can becomes could, will becomes would, may might and must stay the same.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Did you call the office?" she asked. She asked if I ___ the office.
questions.context: A polar question about a past event, reported without backshift.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple becomes the past perfect in reported speech.
Keeping the past simple would leave the two past events without a clear order.
A present perfect would place the call in a period ending now, and the reporting verb is past.
A past continuous would suggest the call was still in progress, which the original question denies.

questions.explanation:
The past simple backshifts to the past perfect. This is what keeps the two past moments in a fixed order in the report.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "How much does the tour cost?" she asked. She asked how much the tour ___.
questions.context: A question about a price, reported with a past reporting verb.

options.feedback: Correct! When the reporting verb is in the present, no backshift is applied and the base form is used.
A would would require a past reporting verb, and she asked in this sentence is the present.
The third person form cannot follow a subject and a reporting verb in a that or wh clause.
Costed is not a form of cost, which does not change in the past simple.

questions.explanation:
No backshift happens when the reporting verb is in the present. She asked how much the tour cost keeps the original tense exactly as it was.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "What were you doing at that time?" he asked. He asked what I ___ doing at that time.
questions.context: A question about a past continuous action, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! A past continuous normally stays unchanged in reported speech.
A present auxiliary would place the action in the present, and at that time refers to the past.
A past perfect would turn an ongoing past action into a completed one and change the meaning.
Did is the auxiliary of the past simple and does not appear with a continuous form.

questions.explanation:
The past continuous is one of the tenses that does not shift. Adding had would change the meaning of the question being reported, so careful speakers keep it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Never seen that film before?" he said. He said he ___ that film before.
questions.context: A question with a negative answer implied, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple in the original becomes the past perfect in the report, and never stays in place.
Keeping the past simple would leave the two events unordered, and the reporting verb is past.
A present perfect would be right with a present reporting verb, but he said is in the past.
Did cannot carry a perfect construction, and never cannot sit between did and the base form.

questions.explanation:
The adverb never is not affected by backshift. What changes is the auxiliary, which becomes had plus not, and the main verb takes its participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Do you have any questions?" the tutor asked. The tutor asked whether we ___ any questions.
questions.context: A question about something someone else owns, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! The do auxiliary backshifts to had and the main verb takes the base form after it.
Keeping do plus have would require a present reporting verb, and the tutor asked is in the past.
A past continuous would describe an action under way, and the original is a simple question.
A would have would build a conditional, and the original question has no such sense.

questions.explanation:
When a simple question uses the auxiliary do, backshift replaces do with did or had and the main verb returns to its base form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Where have you put the keys?" he asked. He asked where I ___ the keys.
questions.context: A question about an object, with the verb in the past perfect.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect backshifts to the past perfect and put keeps its irregular participle.
Keeping the present perfect would require a present reporting verb.
Putted is not a word in English, and put is the same form in the base and the past simple.
A past continuous would suggest the keys were being placed at that moment, which the question denies.

questions.explanation:
Put, cut and let keep the same form in the base, the past simple and the participle. The backshift still applies, so the auxiliary changes but the verb does not.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Why not take the earlier train?" she suggested. She suggested that we ___ the earlier train.
questions.context: A question with a suggestion word, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! Verbs like suggest, recommend and advise take a that clause with should plus base verb.
A would would report a future, but a suggestion is advice about what to do.
Must would express a strict obligation, which is stronger than a suggestion.
A future form would state a fact about the future rather than advice.

questions.explanation:
Reporting verbs such as suggest, insist, recommend and advise are followed by a that clause with should and the base form. This pattern replaces the imperative of the original.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Was the exam hard?" she asked. She asked whether the exam ___ hard.
questions.context: A question about a past state, reported.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple in the direct question backshifts to the past perfect.
Keeping the past simple would leave the two past events without an established order.
A present form would place the exam in the present, and the question is about a finished event.
A future form would predict the difficulty, and the exam is already over.

questions.explanation:
Questions about the past are reported with the past perfect whenever the reporting verb is in the past, exactly as statements about the past are.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "How many pages have you written?" the teacher asked. The teacher asked how many pages I ___.
questions.context: A question asked by a teacher, reported by a student.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect backshifts to the past perfect, and how many is kept.
Keeping the present perfect would require the reporting verb to be present.
The past simple would backshift a past simple, and the original is a present perfect.
A present continuous would describe the action at the moment of speaking, and the question is about a total.

questions.explanation:
A how many question keeps its quantifier and reports exactly like any other wh question, with the tense of the clause backshifted once.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Where are you going?" he asked. "And when will you be back?" He asked where I ___ and when I ___ be back.
questions.context: Two questions reported in sequence.

options.feedback: Correct! Both clauses are backshifted, and the coordinating conjunction joins the two reported questions.
Keeping both original tenses would ignore the past tense of the reporting verb he asked.
A past perfect in the second clause would shift twice, and the original will needs only one step.
The first clause is over-shifted and the second is not shifted at all, which reverses the pattern.

questions.explanation:
Each reported question follows its own backshift rule, independently of the others. Joining them with and or or does not change the tense of either clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She asks where I ___ every weekend.
questions.context: A question reported with the same tense because the reporting verb is present.

options.feedback: Correct! A present reporting verb means no backshift, so the base form is used after the question word.
The past simple would backshift a present simple, and the reporting verb is present.
A present perfect would change the meaning from a routine to a completed visit.
A present continuous would describe a particular journey rather than a weekly habit.

questions.explanation: The tense of the reporting verb decides everything. She asked forces the past perfect, and she asks keeps the original form untouched.
questions.subject: ingles
